item.title: BOJ policymaker Himino warns of upside inflation risks as Japan nears 2% target
item.description:
• Underlying inflation is quite close to BOJ's 2% target
  • Expect underlying inflation to converge to levels consistent with BOJ's target
  • Medium, long-term inflation expectations continue to heighten
  • Financial conditions remain accommodative
  • Real interest rates remain low
  • Delay in adjusting policy could see inflation risks materialise, hurt the economy
  • Upside risks to prices are high

The remarks from BOJ deputy governor, Ryozo Himino, above are not anything that we haven't heard of from the central bank. It mainly juts reinforces the narrative that Japan is getting closer to achieving its long-sought inflation target and that the central bank now has to be careful about letting things run too hot.

The most striking part of his comments is arguably the warning about delaying policy adjustments. But even then, there's no explicit hint that they are going to push for another rate hike sooner rather than later. And that is well reflected in the market pricing as well.

As things stand, traders are virtually ruling out a move at the October meeting but are pricing in roughly 74% odds of another rate hike in December. That is a rather telling contrast, especially when you consider Himino's warning that delaying policy adjustments could allow inflation risks to materialise and ultimately hurt the economy.

That doesn't mean that policymakers are not serious about their remarks. I would say that in Himino's case, his remarks aren't necessarily a push for an October move. Rather, they reinforce the argument that the BOJ cannot afford to sit on its hands for too long. But that's about it. They are neither an explicit confirmation about a move in December as well.

In any case, the takeaway for the yen is that further BOJ tightening remains firmly on the agenda. October may be a foregone conclusion for markets, but December is a different story.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Heads up: UK September CPI inflation report due today, BOE rate hike for November almost fully priced in
item.description:
The UK CPI report for September is the main highlight on the economic calendar today, with the release due at 0600 GMT. The inflation numbers will be heavily watched as it will have a lot to say about what comes next on the BOE outlook, even if traders are almost fully pricing in another 25 bps move in November.

Here's what to expect from the report:

  • Headline CPI: +3.4% y/y expected (Prior +3.1%)
  • Core CPI: +2.8% y/y expected (Prior +2.6%)

The estimates show that another pickup in inflation pressures is expected this time around. That's hardly good news for the BOE with price pressures already running well above its 2% target.

Higher energy costs are expected to remain a key driver, but I would argue that the more important thing to watch today will be the underlying inflation details. In particular, how stubborn services prices will be once again. Any signs of broader price pressures taking hold will only make the BOE's balancing act more difficult.

Looking at market pricing, traders are already pricing in roughly 96% odds of a 25 bps rate hike for 5 November next. As such, I reckon even a hotter inflation reading will do little to change expectations for the immediate decision. Instead, it could strengthen the case for further tightening beyond November. In that lieu, odds of a back-to-back move in December as well are seen at around 61% today. So, how that changes on a hotter-than-expected report will be the crucial point to be mindful of.

On the flip side, a softer-than-expected report could be the more interesting outcome. It might not be enough to derail a November move entirely, but it could see traders pare back some of their more aggressive BOE rate expectations.

Besides that, let's not forget that there is also the autumn budget on 28 October is just around the corner. That will also likely be another key consideration that the BOE has to take into account before their next meeting, aside from the inflation numbers today.

For a more detailed breakdown of the inflation outlook, BOE rate expectations, and budget implications, check out the full UK CPI preview here.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

  • Goldman Sachs now expects the RBA to raise the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on 3 November, having previously forecast no change

  • China’s youth unemployment rate eased to 18% in September from 18.9%
  • The FAA certified Boeing’s 737 MAX 10; SpaceX and Netflix reported results and Super Micro issued a surprise upgrade

Australia: Hauser signals fifth hike risk

Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser delivered the most significant news of the Asian session, signalling that a fifth rate rise this year is a live option at the Board’s next meeting on 3 November.

Speaking at a fireside chat at Citi’s Australia and New Zealand Investment Conference in Sydney, Hauser said the inflation outlook looks worse than the RBA had forecast and that the quarterly trimmed mean, the bank’s preferred measure of underlying inflation, appears set to come in higher than expected. He said capacity pressures in the economy are more elevated than anticipated and that firms are reporting cost pressures as their number one problem.

Hauser stressed that inflation has been high for a very long time and that the RBA cannot allow inflation expectations to drift away from target. He said the bank has to respond to supply shocks to keep expectations anchored, and that while policy cannot target current inflation, that does not mean current inflation is unimportant.

He acknowledged some offsets. September’s labour report was a little weaker than expected, and while unemployment remains quite low, the labour market is easing. Housing data has also slowed, and he said monetary policy is working. Hauser added that forecasts are still being finalised and he does not know for sure what the Board will decide.

Goldman Sachs subsequently changed its call and now expects the RBA to raise the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% in November, having previously forecast a hold. The cash rate stands at 4.60% after the 29 September hike, the fourth of 2026. September-quarter CPI data is due on 28 October, and the decision follows at 2.30pm Sydney time on 3 November (03:30 GMT, 22:30 ET on 2 November).

The Australian dollar rose on Hauser’s remarks but failed to follow through and was little changed on the session.

In equities, NEXTDC shares plunged 44% after the data centre operator cut its FY27 underlying EBITDA guidance to A$245 million to A$265 million, from A$385 million to A$410 million. Grid works for its Melbourne M3 site were suspended after community opposition, pushing additional power supply into FY28. The company froze new development projects.

Japan: December BOJ hike expected

A Reuters poll showed 69% of economists expect the Bank of Japan to raise its policy rate to 1.50% this quarter, with about 80% of those naming a month choosing December rather than the meeting ending 30 October. Most respondents warned that further dissent from government-nominated board members could weigh on the yen.

Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said Japan is on the cusp of sustained, wage-driven inflation and that she sees no gap between the government and the BOJ, after a lawmaker asked whether planned tax cuts could clash with rate hikes.

September exports rose 16.7% year on year, a 13th straight gain driven by AI and chip demand but below the 20.1% forecast. Imports rose 18.9% as delayed crude deliveries trimmed the energy bill, narrowing the trade deficit to ¥536.6 billion, wider than the ¥181 billion expected.

China and South Korea

China’s urban youth unemployment rate, covering 16 to 24-year-olds excluding students, eased to 18% in September from 18.9% in August, which had been the highest reading in 12 months, National Bureau of Statistics data showed.

South Korea’s KOSPI surged more than 5%, with KOSPI 200 futures up 5% triggering a buy-side sidecar that suspended programme trading for five minutes. It was the first such trigger in two months, driven by strong foreign net buying.

Markets

Asian equities were mixed. Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1.1%, while the Shanghai Composite fell 0.4% and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng slipped 0.3%. Oil prices firmed slightly and gold was largely flat.

Corporate: earnings, Boeing and AI

The US Federal Aviation Administration granted final certification to Boeing’s 737 MAX 10, clearing the largest version of its best-selling jet for delivery after nearly seven years of delays and unlocking close to 1,500 orders.

SpaceX reported third-quarter revenue of about $14.6 billion, well above forecasts, with its AI segment contributing more than half. On the earnings call, chief executive Elon Musk said a merger with Tesla would be a good idea but is far from certain, and that AI compute demand is likely to stay strong.

Netflix beat on third-quarter profit but guided fourth-quarter earnings below expectations and lowered its full-year free cash flow forecast to about $12 billion.

Super Micro Computer released a surprise preliminary update lifting September-quarter revenue to $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, far above prior guidance, sending its shares up 14% after hours.

Separately, Nvidia is in talks to invest in Australian AI cloud provider Firmus Grid after it scrapped its IPO, The Information reported, and Citadel founder Ken Griffin said AI is almost certainly in a bubble. Meta Platforms reports after the US close on Wednesday, opening mega-cap tech earnings. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: NEXTDC shares plunge 44% as power delays expose AI data centre bottleneck
item.description:
NEXTDC’s downgrade is a stark example of a risk investors have tended to treat as theoretical: that grid access and local opposition, not customer demand, cap how fast data centre capacity can be built. The read-through extends well beyond Australia, as operators and AI cloud providers globally depend on utilities and planning authorities that move more slowly than hyperscaler spending plans. It echoes the warning in Anthropic’s draft IPO prospectus, reported this week, that resistance to data centres is becoming more organised across jurisdictions. Investors may now apply a larger discount to contracted-but-undelivered capacity across the sector, particularly where projects depend on new grid connections.

-

NEXTDC had the customers and the contracts, but not the electricity, and its 44% share collapse shows the AI build-out now runs only as fast as the local grid and the local council allow.

Summary:

  • NEXTDC shares fell 44% in early trading after the company cut its FY27 guidance
  • Underlying EBITDA guidance was lowered to A$245 million to A$265 million, from A$385 million to A$410 million; net revenue guidance cut to A$475 million to A$500 million, from A$615 million to A$640 million
  • The downgrade stems from delays to grid works by Jemena Electricity Networks for the M3 Melbourne data centre, suspended in September after community opposition, safety concerns and a lack of council consent
  • Works are not expected to restart before February 2027, with extra grid supply now expected in FY28; the affected contracts were worth about A$140 million in prior guidance
  • All new development projects and land purchases are on hold, and FY27 capex guidance was cut to A$4.5 billion to A$5 billion
  • NEXTDC reported about A$8.7 billion of liquidity, including about A$1.3 billion in cash, and remains within its debt covenants

Access to electricity has emerged as a hard limit on the data centre build-out, after Australian operator NEXTDC slashed its earnings forecast because the power needed for a major Melbourne facility will arrive a year later than planned.

NEXTDC shares plunged 44% in early trading after the company cut its fiscal 2027 underlying EBITDA guidance to A$245 million to A$265 million, from A$385 million to A$410 million. Net revenue guidance was lowered to A$475 million to A$500 million, from A$615 million to A$640 million.

The problem is not demand. The capacity at its M3 Melbourne site remains contracted to customers. Instead, grid works being carried out by Jemena Electricity Networks were suspended in September following community and stakeholder opposition, safety concerns and the absence of local council consent while further consultation takes place. Chief executive Craig Scroggie said Jemena did not expect the works to restart before February 2027, pushing the next increase in grid supply to M3 into fiscal 2028.

That delay defers the delivery and billing of contracted capacity that had contributed about A$140 million to both revenue and EBITDA in the previous forecast. The contracts include service-level credits for delays and, in some cases, termination rights.

Planning approval is also slipping. A Victorian government decision on later stages of the M3 development is now expected in 2027, with the state entering caretaker conventions on 3 November ahead of its 28 November election.

NEXTDC has put all new development projects and land acquisitions on hold, focusing spending on capacity due over the next 12 to 18 months, and its board will consider selling development sites not needed in the near term. Fiscal 2027 capex guidance was cut to A$4.5 billion to A$5 billion, from A$5.25 billion to A$5.75 billion. The company said it had about A$8.7 billion of liquidity at 30 September and remains within its financial covenants.

The episode highlights a risk that extends well beyond one company or one city. As AI drives record investment in computing capacity, the pace of delivery increasingly depends on utilities, planners and local communities. Anthropic’s draft IPO prospectus, reported this week, flagged growing and more coordinated political resistance to data centres as a business risk. NEXTDC’s downgrade suggests investors may need to price that risk into contracted capacity across the sector.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia in talks to invest hundreds of millions in Firmus after AI cloud firm’s IPO flop
item.description:
A fresh Nvidia investment would reassure holders of neocloud debt and equity that the sector’s largest supplier remains willing to support it, even as public markets turn more selective. The flip side is that Nvidia backing companies that buy its chips may sharpen questions about how much AI infrastructure demand depends on vendor financing rather than independent capital, an issue that sits at the heart of the bubble debate Ken Griffin revived on Tuesday. For Nvidia shares, the amounts involved are small, so the signal matters more than the money. The episode also suggests the IPO window for AI infrastructure firms is narrowing, pushing more of them toward private and strategic funding.

-

When public investors walked away from Firmus, Nvidia appears ready to step in, a reminder that the AI cloud boom still leans heavily on its biggest supplier.

Summary:

  • Nvidia is in talks to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Firmus Grid, according to The Information, as reported by Bloomberg (gated)
  • The talks follow Firmus’s decision earlier this month to scrap an IPO that would have been one of Australia’s largest
  • Firmus struggled to attract global investors, who have become more cautious on AI companies
  • Nvidia is already an investor in Firmus and several of its peers
  • The move signals continued Nvidia support for neoclouds, a group of heavily indebted AI cloud providers
  • Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment

Nvidia is in talks to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Firmus Grid, an AI cloud company that abandoned its initial public offering earlier this month, The Information reported, according to Bloomberg.

The discussions signal that Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, intends to keep supporting so-called neoclouds, according to the report, which cited people familiar with the talks. Neoclouds are specialist providers that rent out AI computing capacity, competing with the large cloud platforms run by the biggest tech groups. Many have taken on heavy debt to buy chips and build data centres, and the sector has come under pressure as investors grow more cautious.

Nvidia is already an investor in Firmus and in several of its peers. A spokesperson for the company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The talks follow Firmus’s decision to scrap a listing that would have ranked among Australia’s largest. The company struggled to draw global investors, who have become more wary of AI companies, Bloomberg reported. Bloomberg News had previously reported that Firmus was weighing other funding options.

The report adds to a mixed picture for AI infrastructure. On one side, demand signals remain strong: Super Micro Computer this week released a surprise update showing September-quarter revenue far ahead of its own guidance, and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk said compute remains so scarce that older Nvidia chips now rent for more than when new. On the other, public investors are showing more selectivity, and Citadel founder Ken Griffin said on Tuesday that AI is almost certainly in a bubble.

Nvidia’s willingness to back customers that buy its chips supports the neocloud model in the short term, but it also raises questions about how much of the sector’s growth relies on its main supplier. The size and terms of any Firmus investment, and whether other backers join, will indicate how much confidence remains in the neocloud business outside Nvidia itself.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US intel says Putin ordered NATO sabotage drive, Leipzig drone attack an opening shot
item.description:
The report raises the perceived risk of escalation between Russia and NATO, which would tend to support European defence stocks and weigh on European risk sentiment if officials respond with tougher measures. The energy channel is the one to watch: Russia’s diesel supply deal with Washington and the pause in new US sanctions were aimed partly at keeping Moscow out of the war with Iran, so any rupture in that arrangement could tighten fuel markets already strained by the Middle East conflict. Drone strikes on commercial ships in the Black Sea add a shipping risk premium near NATO waters. For now, the report adds detail and attribution rather than a new event, so the market impact may be limited unless governments act on it.

-

The Leipzig attack was already pinned on Russian military intelligence, but the WSJ’s reporting moves the responsibility up to Putin himself and shows how close Germany came to invoking NATO’s mutual defence clause.

Summary:

  • US intelligence agencies say Putin directly ordered an intensified campaign of sabotage and covert action against NATO countries, according to European officials cited by the Wall Street Journal (gated) 
  • The failed August drone attack on a cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig-Halle Airport was one of the campaign’s opening shots, they said
  • Aides to Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany would have considered invoking NATO’s Article 5 had the attack caused heavy casualties
  • Western intelligence traced the operation to a unit of Russia’s military intelligence, with logistics run through Serbia, where seven suspects have since been arrested
  • A Kremlin back-channel contact warned Berlin after the attack that it would not be the last
  • Russia denies involvement in sabotage in Europe

US intelligence agencies have concluded that Russian President Vladimir Putin personally ordered a stepped-up campaign of sabotage and covert action against NATO countries, with a failed drone attack on a German airport in August among its first operations, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing European officials briefed on the findings.

The attack at Leipzig-Halle Airport, one of Europe’s largest air-cargo hubs, targeted an Antonov freighter used to carry military aid to Ukraine. Germany formally blamed Russia for the attempt in September. The Journal’s reporting goes further, placing the order at the top of the Kremlin and framing Leipzig as part of a deliberate escalation.

Aides to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the newspaper that had the attack caused large numbers of casualties, Berlin would have considered invoking Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, the collective-defence clause that obliges allies to come to a member’s aid. It has been invoked only once, after the September 11 attacks in 2001.

According to investigators cited by the Journal, at least three drones loaded with Semtex were hidden near the airport perimeter and controlled remotely through German mobile networks. One struck the freighter without exploding. German cyber officials traced the communications to servers previously used by Russia’s military intelligence agency.

Western officials attributed the campaign to a GRU branch known as the Special Tasks Service, formed in 2023, and traced the Leipzig plot to one of its department chiefs, already under EU and UK sanctions. Investigators believe a former Russian officer coordinated the ground logistics with Belarusian operatives, using Serbia as a hub to move drones and explosives. Serbian prosecutors have since arrested seven suspects.

The report said European officials have seen a sharp rise in so-called grey-zone attacks since August, including arson against drone makers in Estonia and Poland, sabotage of Starlink stations in Poland, Lithuania and Bulgaria, and drone strikes on merchant ships in the Black Sea. After the Leipzig attempt, a Kremlin back-channel contact reportedly warned Berlin that more attacks would follow.

Russia has denied involvement, with Putin questioning in September where the evidence was. The Kremlin did not respond to the Journal’s request for comment.

The findings come as Washington pursues a delicate relationship with Moscow, including a diesel supply arrangement and a pause in new sanctions that President Donald Trump has said is aimed at keeping Russia out of the war with Iran. How European governments respond, and whether Washington adjusts its approach, will be the next test. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan’s Katayama sees no gap with BOJ, says wage-driven inflation is near
item.description:
Katayama’s comments may ease some of the political risk flagged in today’s Reuters poll, where most economists warned that dissent from government-nominated BOJ board members could weigh on the yen. Her description of an economy close to wage-driven inflation is language that supports the case for further tightening, which would tend to support the yen and keep upward pressure on short-dated JGB yields. Her reference to import-driven price rises also keeps oil in focus, with energy costs tied to the Middle East conflict a direct driver of Japan’s inflation. The tension between consumption tax cuts and BOJ tightening remains, and markets may test her “no gap” message against how board members vote at the next hike.

-

Katayama’s message was that fiscal support and monetary tightening can coexist, but the real test of “no gap” will come when the BOJ next votes.

Summary:

  • Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said Japan is seeing price rises driven by higher import costs
  • She said the economy is on the cusp of a shift to sustained inflation driven by rising wages
  • The planned consumption tax cut and payouts are aimed at cushioning households from rising living costs, she told parliament
  • Asked whether the tax cut could conflict with BOJ rate hikes, she said the government and BOJ are exchanging views and she sees no gap between them
  • The comments come as most economists expect the BOJ to raise rates to 1.50% in December

Japan’s Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Wednesday that the economy is on the cusp of a shift to sustained inflation driven by rising wages, and that she sees no gap between the government’s views and those of the Bank of Japan.

Speaking in parliament, Katayama said Japan is currently experiencing price rises driven largely by higher import costs. She said the economy is close to moving into a period where inflation is sustained by wage growth, a transition the BOJ has long described as a condition for normalising monetary policy.

Katayama said the government’s planned consumption tax cut and household payouts are intended to cushion the impact of rising living costs. Asked by a lawmaker whether the tax cut could work against the central bank’s efforts to tame inflation through rate hikes, she said the government and the BOJ are exchanging views on various fronts and that she sees no gap between their positions.

The question reflects a tension markets have been watching closely. Fiscal measures that support household spending can add to demand at a time when the BOJ is tightening policy, and investors have been alert to signs of political resistance to further rate rises. In September, two board members nominated by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government voted against the decision to raise rates to 1.25%, briefly weakening the yen.

A Reuters poll published on Wednesday found most economists expect the BOJ to raise its policy rate to 1.50% in December, keeping up a quarterly pace of increases. Nearly three-quarters said further dissenting votes at the next hike could weigh on the yen, which remains only modestly above its 2026 low.

Katayama’s remarks may help reassure markets that the government is not pushing against tightening, although she did not explicitly endorse further rate rises. Import costs, including energy prices tied to the Middle East conflict, remain a key driver of the inflation she described.

The BOJ’s next policy meeting ends on 30 October, when it will publish fresh growth and inflation forecasts. Attention will then shift to December, where the vote split may prove as important as the decision itself. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan exports rise 16.7% for 13th straight month on AI chip demand, trade gap narrows
item.description:
The trade data is broadly supportive for the yen and for the BOJ’s tightening case, with exports still growing strongly and firms passing higher costs through to prices. The narrowing deficit owes much to oil disruption rather than weaker demand: Houthi rerouting delayed crude arrivals, so the import bill is likely to rebound in October as Suez-routed tankers arrive and procurement returns to around year-earlier levels. That makes oil prices and Middle East shipping the key swing factor for Japan’s trade balance and the yen’s import-driven pressure in the months ahead. For the BOJ, solid external demand adds to the case for a December hike, with its 30 October meeting and fresh forecasts the next focus.

Japan’s exporters are still riding the AI boom, but September’s narrower trade gap owes more to delayed oil tankers than to any lasting improvement.

Summary:

  • Trade balance (Sep): deficit of ¥536.6 billion vs ¥181 billion expected; prior ¥1,111.9 billion
  • Exports (Sep y/y): +16.7% vs +20.1% expected; prior +19.3%
  • Imports (Sep y/y): +18.9% vs +19.6% expected; prior +28.0%
  • Exports rose for a 13th straight month, driven by semiconductors and AI-related products and by firms passing on higher costs
  • Exports to the US rose 22.9%; shipments to China gained 8.6%
  • Import growth slowed as crude deliveries were delayed by tanker rerouting away from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait; the government expects crude procurement to recover to around year-earlier levels in October

Japan’s exports rose 16.7% in September from a year earlier, extending their run of gains to 13 consecutive months as strong demand for semiconductors and AI-related products offset weakness elsewhere, Ministry of Finance data showed on Wednesday.

The increase fell short of the 20.1% rise economists had expected and followed a 19.3% gain in August, but export growth remained robust. Solid global investment in artificial intelligence continued to support shipments of chips and related equipment, while companies’ efforts to pass higher costs on through prices also lifted the value of exports.

By destination, exports to the United States jumped 22.9% from a year earlier, and shipments to China rose 8.6%.

Imports climbed 18.9%, slightly below the 19.6% forecast and slower than August’s 28% surge. Oil was the main factor. Crude arrivals dropped after tankers rerouted away from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, when Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi militia declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, delaying deliveries to Japan.

The softer import bill helped narrow the trade deficit to ¥536.6 billion, about $3.4 billion, from roughly ¥1.1 trillion in August. That was still considerably wider than the ¥181 billion shortfall economists had forecast.

The relief on imports is likely to prove temporary. The government said crude procurement in October is expected to recover to around 100% of the level a year earlier, as tankers travelling via the Suez Canal reach Japan, which would push the energy import bill back up.

The figures suggest external demand remains a support for Japan’s economy, although uncertainty over the global outlook continues to cloud the picture for exporters.

Attention now turns to the Bank of Japan’s policy meeting ending on 30 October, where it will publish fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts. Markets will scrutinise those projections for clues on the timing of the next rate rise, which most economists expect in December. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6779 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through October, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run.--- The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.Summary:
  • The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets. 
  • China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, allowing the yuan to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the daily midpoint during onshore hours. 
  • The midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the prior day's close, moves in major currencies, broader international FX conditions and domestic factors such as capital flows and growth momentum, with policymakers retaining discretion over the final number. 
  • If market pressure pushes the yuan toward either edge of the band, the PBOC can intervene through direct buying or selling of yuan, liquidity adjustments, or guidance via state-owned banks. 
  • A stronger-than-expected fixing typically signals the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can indicate tolerance for a softer currency or discomfort with the pace of gains. 
  • For nearly a year the fixing has been set weaker than market estimates, with the gap reaching its widest since February in late August. 
  • In October the midpoint reached its strongest level since February 2023. 
  • The yuan has pushed to its strongest levels since early 2023 onshore and since mid-2022 offshore
The People's Bank of China sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT, a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. It has taken on added significance in recent weeks as policymakers have shifted from restraining the yuan's rise to guiding it higher.China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the yuan is allowed to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the central midpoint set each trading day. That midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies such as the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic considerations like capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The calculation is not purely mechanical, giving policymakers room to use the fixing to guide market expectations.Once the midpoint is set, onshore USD/CNY trades freely within the allowable range. Should market pressure push the currency toward either edge of that band, the central bank can step in to smooth volatility, whether through direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance channelled through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often read as a policy signal rather than a purely technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected midpoint typically suggests the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can signal tolerance for a softer currency, or unease with how quickly the yuan is rising.That second reading has dominated for much of the past year. For nearly a year, the central bank set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, a pattern traders and analysts interpreted as an attempt to slow the yuan's appreciation. The gap reached its widest since February in late August, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high against the dollar.September has brought a clear change of tone. The midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace this month, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the PBOC has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The central bank strengthened the fixing for eight consecutive sessions, the longest streak since 2023, and the midpoint has since reached its strongest level since February 2023. The onshore yuan has traded at its strongest since January 2023, while the offshore rate has reached levels last seen in July 2022. Even so, the fixing is still being set well weaker than market estimates, with one recent midpoint more than 500 pips below a Reuters survey forecast, a reminder that Beijing is allowing appreciation on its own terms rather than stepping aside.The timing has been linked to diplomacy.

The underlying tension is a familiar one. A firmer yuan supports capital stability and eases import costs, but a rapid rise risks undermining export competitiveness at a moment when China's broader economy continues to show signs of softness. For traders and investors, the gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest windows into how Beijing is weighing that trade-off, and whether the recent green light for gains stays in place once the summit has passed.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Citadel’s Griffin says AI “almost certainly” a bubble, even as demand signals stay strong
item.description:
A bubble call from one of the most closely watched figures in finance is likely to sharpen the debate over AI valuations, though Griffin’s framing stops well short of a call to exit. His argument that transformative shifts usually come with a bubble implies volatility and losers along the way, not a collapse in the underlying trend, which may limit any direct market reaction. The timing is notable: his comments arrived alongside SpaceX’s AI revenue beat, Super Micro’s surprise upgrade and Musk’s claim that compute remains scarce, so investors are weighing strong near-term demand against concerns about how much of it is already priced in. That tension may feed the stock-specific volatility analysts expect this earnings season.

Griffin thinks AI is both a bubble and the real thing, which is less a contradiction than a reminder that the dot-com bust still left Amazon standing.

Summary:

  • Citadel founder Ken Griffin said investors are almost certainly in an AI bubble
  • He argued that any radical transformation of the economy is generally intertwined with a bubble
  • Griffin compared the moment to the dot-com era and its fanciful business models, adding he wished he had kept his Amazon shares
  • He spoke at the Future of Global Markets Conference in New York on Tuesday
  • His views on AI have shifted through 2026, from dismissive at Davos in January to unsettled by its capabilities in May
  • The comments came on a day of strong AI demand signals from SpaceX, Super Micro and Elon Musk

Ken Griffin, the billionaire founder of hedge fund Citadel and market maker Citadel Securities, said investors are almost certainly in an artificial intelligence bubble, offering a sceptical counterpoint on a day of strong AI demand signals.

Speaking at the Future of Global Markets Conference in New York on Tuesday, Griffin argued that radical transformations of the economy tend to be tied up with bubbles. He pointed to the period before the dot-com crash, when some business models proved fanciful, but also to the companies that endured, remarking that he wished he had held on to his Amazon shares at the time.

That framing matters. Griffin was not dismissing AI as hype. His argument was that a genuine technological shift and a speculative bubble can coexist, with excess valuations and failed ventures alongside lasting winners.

His remarks mark the latest turn in a shifting stance through 2026. At Davos early in the year, he was openly dismissive of AI. By May, speaking at Stanford’s business school, he said he was unsettled by how much the technology could achieve. His latest comments sit between those positions, accepting AI’s transformative potential while warning that markets have run ahead of it.

The timing gave his view added weight. Earlier in the session, SpaceX reported AI revenue of about $7.6 billion, more than half its quarterly total, and chief executive Elon Musk said compute was so scarce that older Nvidia chips now rent for more than when new. Super Micro Computer separately released a preliminary update showing September-quarter revenue far ahead of its own guidance.

Those data points suggest demand is real and, for now, accelerating. Griffin’s warning is about price rather than demand: whether the valuations attached to AI-linked companies reflect realistic outcomes for all of them.

With mega-cap tech earnings season under way, starting with Meta, investors will be looking for evidence on that question, particularly whether heavy AI spending is beginning to generate returns that support current valuations.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: SpaceX’s Musk says Tesla merger good idea but far from certain, needs 50% of Tesla shares
item.description:
The merger remark is likely to draw the most attention, particularly for Tesla shareholders, though Musk’s own caveats suggest it is an idea rather than a plan, which may limit any sustained move. Requiring approval from half of all Tesla shares sets a high bar, so investors may treat the comment as a long-dated possibility rather than a near-term catalyst. The compute comments are a cleaner read-through: a claim that older Nvidia H100 chips now rent for more than when new points to tight supply across AI infrastructure, which would tend to support sentiment toward Nvidia, server makers and AI cloud providers. Coming on the same session as Super Micro’s surprise upgrade, it adds to a run of strong AI demand signals.

Musk floated a SpaceX-Tesla merger while stressing it may never happen, but his clearer message was that AI compute remains so scarce that even older chips are rising in value.

Summary:

  • SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on the company’s earnings call that a merger with Tesla would be a good idea but is far from certain
  • He said any deal would need shareholder support, including approval from 50% of all Tesla shares
  • Musk said demand for AI compute is likely to remain strong
  • He said older Nvidia H100 chips are now renting for more than when they were new
  • He warned a shortage of compute for superintelligence could persist for a long time
  • The comments follow SpaceX’s quarterly results, in which AI revenue beat forecasts and made up more than half of sales

More from SpaceX’s earnings call, where chief executive Elon Musk said a merger between SpaceX and Tesla would be a good idea but cautioned that it is far from certain, while also signalling that demand for AI computing power shows no sign of easing.

Musk said any combination would require shareholder support, including approval from 50% of all Tesla shares. The reference to all shares suggests a threshold based on total shares outstanding rather than only those voted, which would set a considerably higher bar. He gave no indication of a proposal, a timetable or any formal talks, and his comments are best read as a view on a possible future structure rather than a deal in progress.

On AI, Musk said demand for compute is likely to remain strong. He said older Nvidia H100 chips are currently renting for more than they did when new, a sign, in his view, of how tight the supply of AI processing capacity has become. He also warned that a shortage of the compute needed to develop superintelligence could last for a long time.

The comments add context to SpaceX’s third-quarter results, released earlier in the session. Revenue of about $14.6 billion beat forecasts, with the AI segment contributing about $7.6 billion, or more than half the total. Capital spending of about $19.6 billion, most of it directed at AI, exceeded quarterly revenue, so Musk’s view that compute will stay scarce helps explain why the company continues to invest at that pace.

The remarks also landed on the same day Super Micro Computer released a surprise preliminary update showing September-quarter revenue well ahead of its own guidance, adding to evidence that spending on AI infrastructure remains robust.

For now, the merger idea looks like a long-term possibility with significant hurdles, while the compute message is more immediately relevant for investors tracking the AI hardware trade. Any further detail from Musk or either company on the merger would be the next thing to watch.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS flags 3 tests for the AI trade as Meta kicks off mega-cap tech earnings
item.description:
With rates rising and financing costs higher, the tolerance for open-ended AI spending is narrowing, which puts capex guidance at the centre of market reaction this season. Any sign that spending is outpacing revenue could hit hyperscaler shares even on headline beats, while firm commitments to sustained investment would tend to support semiconductor and AI hardware names further up the supply chain. UBS’s warning about company-specific volatility suggests results may produce sharper winners and losers than the broad AI trade has seen. Meta’s report sets the early tone, as an advertising-led business funding heavy AI investment.

Earlier:

  • Stock earnings pick of the week: Meta faces a $145 billion question after the tech rout
  • What is earnings season and why the first companies to report are important to watch

UBS says the AI trade has moved past the adoption story: this earnings season, big tech has to show the spending is turning into revenue, profit and returns.

Summary:

  • Meta’s results after the US close on Wednesday open the reporting season for mega-cap tech
  • UBS says rising rates and higher financing costs put AI monetisation and capex returns under closer scrutiny
  • Its three tests: health of core businesses, AI monetisation beyond adoption, and tangible returns on infrastructure spending
  • UBS expects a strong third quarter fundamentally but warns elevated expectations may cause company-specific volatility
  • It remains constructive on the structural AI opportunity, favouring hyperscalers and high-quality semiconductor and hardware beneficiaries

Big US technology companies need to show this earnings season that artificial intelligence can generate returns large enough to justify heavy capital spending, according to UBS, which has set out three tests that it says could shape the AI trade into 2027.

Meta Platforms opens mega-cap tech reporting when it releases third-quarter results after the US close on Wednesday, with its conference call at 4.30pm ET (20:30 GMT). UBS said rising interest rates and higher financing costs mean investors are looking harder at whether AI can drive meaningful revenue while capital spending weighs on free cash flow. The bank did not take a view on any single company.

The first test is the health of core businesses. UBS said the largest tech groups enter the season with strong positions in advertising, software, devices and digital commerce, and that continued demand in those areas helps fund AI investment while cushioning earnings. The question is whether recent growth can hold up as year-on-year comparisons get tougher and economic risks persist.

The second is monetisation. Rising use of AI products is encouraging, UBS said, but investors increasingly want evidence that usage translates into revenue and profit, whether through subscriptions, consumption-based pricing, advertising, transactions or greater cloud utilisation. Clarity on pricing and customer willingness to pay would strengthen the case that AI is becoming a revenue driver rather than mainly an investment programme.

The third is returns on spending. Even if AI revenue grows, the scale of infrastructure investment has implications for margins and cash flow. UBS said investors will focus on capacity utilisation, pricing power, capital requirements and returns on AI investment, with management commentary on the future pace of capex likely to shape expectations for 2027 and beyond.

Overall, UBS expects a strong quarter from a fundamental perspective but cautioned that elevated expectations could produce company-specific volatility. It remains constructive on the long-term AI opportunity, seeing value in hyperscalers and high-quality semiconductor and hardware companies, while suggesting investors with concentrated tech holdings consider rebalancing across sectors and regions during periods of strength.

With Meta first up and other mega-cap names following in the coming weeks, capex guidance is likely to matter as much as the quarterly numbers themselves.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Super Micro shares jump 14% as preliminary revenue tops forecast by about $4 billion
item.description:
The update gives the AI hardware trade a fresh demand signal, and the after-hours moves in Dell and HPE show investors treating it as a read-through for the wider server group rather than a company-specific win. That matters given both stocks fell heavily last week, so the rebound may test whether that selling was overdone. The margin beat could carry more weight than the revenue figure, as it eases a long-running concern that Super Micro has had to trade profitability for volume. With limited detail until 3 November, the open question is customer concentration: how much of the surge comes from the large cloud providers versus newer AI-focused buyers, whose spending may be less durable.

Super Micro did not just sell far more AI servers than expected, it kept more of the money from each one, and that combination briefly lifted the whole server sector.

Summary:

  • Super Micro released a surprise preliminary update for the September quarter, ahead of full results on 3 November
  • Revenue is now expected at $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, against prior guidance of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion and analyst expectations of about $15 billion
  • The midpoint implies revenue growth of nearly 280% from a year earlier
  • Gross margin is estimated at 12% to 12.5%, above the previous 10.4% to 10.8% outlook
  • Super Micro shares rose 14% in extended trading; Dell gained 6% and HPE 5%
  • The split of sales between major cloud companies and newer AI cloud providers is not yet known

Super Micro Computer shares jumped 14% in extended trading on Tuesday after the AI server maker released a surprise preliminary update showing September-quarter revenue and profitability well ahead of its own guidance and Wall Street expectations.

The company now expects revenue of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion for the quarter, compared with its earlier forecast of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion. Analysts tracked by FactSet had expected about $15 billion. The midpoint of the new range points to growth of nearly 280% from the same quarter a year earlier, a pace that reflects heavy spending on AI computing infrastructure.

Profitability, a recurring concern for Super Micro investors, also improved. The company estimates gross margin of 12% to 12.5% for the quarter, above its previous outlook of 10.4% to 10.8%. Gross margin measures how much revenue a company keeps after covering the direct costs of making its products. Super Micro’s margins remain thin by technology hardware standards, but the improvement suggests it is gaining some pricing power in a market where rival Dell Technologies has historically commanded a premium on AI servers.

Analysts described the update as a positive sign for AI compute demand, and one noted that the combination of stronger sales and better margins bodes well for other server makers. Dell shares rose 6% after hours and Hewlett Packard Enterprise gained 5%, recovering some ground after heavy losses last week.

The release came on a busy day for technology investors, landing alongside SpaceX’s quarterly results, which also showed strong AI-related revenue.

Super Micro’s update was brief, covering only a handful of figures with little commentary. One key unknown, analysts said, is how much of the quarter’s business came from the major cloud providers compared with newer AI-focused cloud companies such as CoreWeave and SpaceX. That mix will shape how investors judge the durability of the growth.

A fuller picture is due when Super Micro reports official results on 3 November, when investors will look for guidance on whether the current quarter can sustain the pace.

item.title: Goldman Sachs says 6% nominal growth, not 5% yields, is what matters for small caps
item.description:

The flip side is that the thesis is explicitly tied to nominal growth, so small caps may become more sensitive to economic data surprises than to moves in yields, with a softer PMI or GDP print a bigger threat than a rate rise. Goldman’s view that inflation pressure is largely energy-driven also links the outlook to oil: a further spike in crude would test the argument that broader inflation is moderating. The emphasis on dispersion suggests index-level small-cap exposure may lag a more selective approach.

-

Earlier:

  • SpaceX beats Q3 forecasts across all three segments as AI revenue tops $7.5 billion

-

Goldman Sachs argues small-cap investors are watching the wrong number: the growth backdrop, not the 10-year yield, is what decides whether the asset class works.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says the key question for small caps is whether nominal growth stays healthy, not whether the 10-year yield is above 5%
  • Small caps have historically done best when nominal GDP is above 5% and accelerating; it is currently running near 6%, with real GDP around 2.3%
  • The bank notes small caps have generally delivered positive returns during periods of sharply rising rates
  • It expects U.S. growth of about 2.3%, unemployment near 4% and contained recession risk, with PMIs at their highest in more than five years
  • Inflation looks narrower than headline figures suggest, with much of the pressure energy-related
  • Valuations look attractive versus large caps and history, and a higher cost of capital should favour active stock selection

Goldman Sachs says investors weighing small-cap stocks should focus less on the level of interest rates and more on the strength of nominal economic growth, arguing in a new note that the growth backdrop currently favours the asset class.

The bank said the central question is not whether the 10-year Treasury yield sits above 5%, but whether nominal growth remains healthy. Small caps have historically performed best when nominal GDP, which combines real growth and inflation, is above 5% and accelerating, according to Goldman Sachs. Nominal GDP is currently running near 6% year on year, with real GDP at around 2.3%.

Goldman Sachs said higher rates alone have not historically been a reason to avoid small caps, noting the group has generally posted positive returns during periods of sharply rising rates.

The bank’s macro outlook supports that view. It expects U.S. growth of about 2.3%, unemployment near 4% and relatively contained recession risk, while purchasing managers’ indices have reached their highest levels in more than five years. Goldman Sachs also said inflation looks narrower than headline figures suggest, with much of the pressure coming from energy and broader measures continuing to moderate.

On fundamentals, the bank said earnings strength among smaller companies appears to be broadening rather than concentrating in a handful of names. It described valuations as attractive relative to both large caps and historical levels, offering what it sees as a compelling entry point alongside improving fundamentals.

Goldman Sachs added that a rising cost of capital raises the bar for companies, rewarding profitability, durable earnings and strong returns on capital while penalising weaker businesses. That widening gap between winners and losers, it said, may create a more favourable environment for stock picking and active management.

The argument rests on growth holding up. If nominal GDP slows meaningfully, or energy-driven inflation broadens into wider price pressure that forces rates higher still, the conditions Goldman Sachs identifies as supportive for small caps would weaken. For now, the bank sees the growth backdrop doing more of the work than the rate debate suggests.

-

Hauser has all but previewed a hot underlying inflation print, and with capacity tighter than assumed and supply shocks no longer something to look through, a softer jobs market looks like a footnote rather than a reprieve.

  • He said capacity pressures in the economy are more elevated than anticipated

Speaking at Citi’s Australia and New Zealand Investment Conference in Sydney, Hauser said the quarterly trimmed mean appeared set to be higher than the RBA had expected. Hauser also said capacity pressures in the economy were more elevated than the RBA had anticipated, suggesting demand is still running further ahead of supply than policymakers assumed.

item.title: BOJ seen lifting rates to 1.50% in December as 69% of economists expect a Q4 hike
item.description:
The poll firms up December as the likely window for the BOJ’s next move, which should limit yen sensitivity to the 30 October meeting but raises the stakes around the December decision. The bigger currency risk may be the vote itself: with the yen only modestly above its 2026 low, a repeat of September’s dissent from government-nominated board members could be read as political resistance to tightening and trigger fresh selling. Rising energy and import costs tied to the Middle East war keep oil a direct input into Japan’s inflation outlook, so a further jump in crude would likely harden the case for hikes. For JGBs, the shift toward a 2% or higher terminal rate, combined with fiscal concerns, points to continued pressure on yields.

-

Economists now broadly expect the BOJ to keep raising rates every quarter, with the main risk to the yen coming not from the timing of the next move but from who votes against it.

Summary:

  • 69% of economists (54 of 78) in an October 13 to 19 Reuters poll expect the BOJ to lift its policy rate to 1.50% this quarter, up from 36% in September
  • Of those naming a month, about 80% picked December; only 2% chose the meeting ending 30 October
  • 60% expect the rate to reach 1.75% by end-June 2027; 51% now see a terminal rate of 2.00% or higher, up from 40% in September
  • Nearly three-quarters said further dissent at the next hike could weigh on the yen, which is only about 4% above its 2026 low near 164 per dollar
  • Nearly two-thirds expect the government to keep new bond issuance below 40 trillion yen for fiscal 2027

The Bank of Japan is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate to 1.50% in December, according to a Reuters poll of economists, extending a pattern of quarterly increases after hikes in June and September.

Of 78 economists surveyed between 13 and 19 October, 54, or nearly 70%, expected a move to 1.50% this quarter, almost double the share in the September poll. About 80% of those naming a month chose December, while just 2% expected action at the BOJ’s two-day meeting ending on 30 October.

Higher energy and import costs, made worse by a weak yen and the war in the Middle East, are adding to inflation pressure, the poll found. A period of relative stability in the yen, which faced heavy selling for much of the year and prompted intervention from both Japanese authorities and the US Treasury, also supports the case for a December move. Board member Junko Koeda said last week the BOJ should not become overly cautious about raising rates, now at their highest in 31 years, given significant upside risks to inflation.

Not every economist sees the need for speed. Some argued the economy is not overheating enough to justify back-to-back hikes and that prices remain within the BOJ’s expected range. Sources have told Reuters that many BOJ officials want more data on how earlier increases have affected financial conditions.

Expectations for the peak rate have shifted higher. Sixty per cent of respondents saw the policy rate at 1.75% by the end of June next year, while the share expecting it to reach 2.00% or more rose to 51% from 40% in September.

Politics remains a risk for the yen. In September, two board members nominated by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who favour looser fiscal policy, voted against raising rates to 1.25%. Nearly three-quarters of economists said further dissent at the next hike could weigh on the yen, which sits only about 4% above its 2026 low near 164 per dollar.

On fiscal policy, nearly two-thirds of respondents expected the government to keep new bond issuance below 40 trillion yen, about $250 billion, for fiscal 2027, after Takaichi said she aims to hold issuance around that level.

With the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank also expected to raise rates in December, according to separate Reuters polls, the BOJ’s next decision will be judged as much on the vote split as on the move itself.

A personal note: I write article after article on the Bank of Japan outlook and every shift in economists’ views, but if I had simply written “a quarterly pace of rate rises” and left it at that, I reckon I’d have been 99% correct.

item.title: JPMorgan sees Bitcoin returning 10% a year: why volatility makes that hard to collect
item.description:
JPMorgan expects Bitcoin to return 10% a year. Here is why that number is harder to hold than it looks

J.P. Morgan Asset Management has put a long-term return forecast on Bitcoin for the first time. Its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, the 31st edition of the firm’s annual 10 to 15 year outlook, project a compound return of about 10% a year, according to reports on the document. That is higher than the firm’s 7.5% forecast for US large-cap stocks. JPMorgan has not added Bitcoin to its main portfolio models, though, and the reason it gives is the most useful lesson in the report.

What JPMorgan actually said

The firm says that for the first time it has put a range on Bitcoin returns. It has not included Bitcoin in its main covariance matrices, the models it uses to estimate how assets move together when building portfolios. Instead, it built a separate, smaller set comparing Bitcoin with a subset of public-market assets.

JPMorgan said Bitcoin’s volatility and unstable correlations with other assets remain an obstacle to wider portfolio inclusion. Reports on the document put its volatility assumption at about 55% a year, against roughly 18% for US large-cap stocks. The analysts said they could revisit the approach if volatility falls and correlations settle, particularly as regulation, liquidity and price discovery improve.

So this is a forecast, not an allocation. JPMorgan is telling clients what it expects Bitcoin might return, not recommending they own it.

The lesson: average returns and compound returns are not the same

Long-term forecasts like this one are usually quoted as compound returns, the rate at which money actually grows over time. That is different from the simple average of yearly returns, and the gap between the two widens as volatility rises.

A simple example shows why. Imagine two investments, each with an average return of 10% a year over two years. The first gains 10% in year one and 10% in year two. A $100 stake grows to $121. The second gains 60% in year one and then loses 40% in year two. The average is still 10%, but the $100 becomes $160 and then $96. The investor has lost money.

This effect is often called volatility drag. Large losses do more damage than equally large gains repair, because a fall applies to a bigger or smaller base than the rise before it. A common rule of thumb is that the compound return sits below the average return by roughly half the variance, the square of volatility.

For an asset with 18% volatility, that drag is modest, about 1.6 percentage points. At 55% volatility, the same rule of thumb suggests a gap of roughly 15 percentage points. In other words, for Bitcoin to compound at 10% a year at that level of volatility, its average yearly return would need to be far higher. Treat that as an illustration of the mechanism rather than JPMorgan’s own arithmetic.

Why this matters for investors

The headline comparison, 10% for Bitcoin against 7.5% for US stocks, compares compound returns but not the ride. An investor who sells after a deep drawdown may never collect the long-term compound figure at all. Position size matters for the same reason. A small allocation to a highly volatile asset can be held through large swings; a large one is far harder to sit through.

This is also why JPMorgan’s correlation caveat matters. Portfolio models rely on assets behaving in reasonably predictable ways relative to each other. If Bitcoin sometimes trades like a technology stock and sometimes on its own, it is hard to say how much it diversifies a portfolio, and the firm says that instability impairs a strategic allocation.

There is a countercase. Bitwise chief investment officer Matt Hougan welcomed the forecast but argued that a 55% volatility assumption is too high, pointing to Bitcoin’s falling volatility over the past 15 years. If he is right, the drag would be smaller and the case for an allocation stronger.

What to watch next

  • Bitcoin’s realized volatility. A sustained fall would be the clearest sign that JPMorgan’s main obstacle is easing.
  • Correlation behavior. Watch whether Bitcoin keeps moving with the Nasdaq during risk-off periods or starts to trade more independently.
  • Next year’s LTCMA. If JPMorgan moves Bitcoin into its main covariance matrices, that would be the shift from forecasting to modeling, and a far stronger signal than the 10% figure.

The practical takeaway: a high expected return does not tell you whether you can hold an asset long enough to earn it. Volatility decides that, and for now JPMorgan thinks Bitcoin’s volatility is still too high.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Anthropic IPO draft shows nearly 15-fold revenue jump and $600 billion in compute deals
item.description:
The commitments disclosed in the filing amount to multi-year revenue visibility for Anthropic’s infrastructure suppliers, with Google, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Broadcom each tied to contracts running into the tens or hundreds of billions of dollars, much of it noncancelable. That may support the case that AI infrastructure demand is contracted rather than speculative, though it also concentrates counterparty risk on a single loss-making buyer. For prospective IPO investors, the debate is likely to centre on whether revenue growth can keep outrunning compute costs, and on customer concentration, with two clients contributing around a fifth of first-half sales. A valuation of up to $2 trillion would leave little room for a slowdown on either front.

Anthropic’s draft prospectus shows a company growing faster than its costs, but committed to an infrastructure bill so large that its suppliers, customers and regulators all become part of the investment case.

Summary:

  • First-half 2026 revenue of about $16.3 billion, up from about $1.1 billion a year earlier, according to a draft prospectus viewed by the Wall Street Journal (gated)
  • Net loss of about $81 billion for the half, of which roughly $72 billion came from accounting charges tied to convertible notes and other financing instruments; the prior-year half-year loss was about $13 billion
  • Compute and infrastructure spending of nearly $9 billion in the half, more than in all of 2025
  • Infrastructure commitments exceed $600 billion, with further deals under negotiation that could add up to $150 billion
  • Around a fifth of first-half revenue came from two customers
  • Risk factors include AI safety and liability, possible uninsurable catastrophic incidents, constrained compute access and organised opposition to data centres

Anthropic grew revenue nearly fifteenfold in the first half of 2026 while committing to more than $600 billion in future computing infrastructure, according to a draft initial public offering prospectus reviewed by the Wall Street Journal. The company declined to comment on the report.

The artificial intelligence developer generated about $16.3 billion in revenue in the six months to 30 June, compared with about $1.1 billion a year earlier, the Journal reported. That is already well above the roughly $4.6 billion it brought in during all of 2025. Spending on computing capacity and infrastructure rose to nearly $9 billion in the half, from about $2.3 billion a year earlier, and exceeded the company’s full-year 2025 outlay of around $7.3 billion.

The headline loss is far larger. Anthropic recorded a net loss of about $81 billion for the half, against roughly $13 billion a year earlier and about $42 billion for the whole of 2025. Around $72 billion of that reflected accounting charges linked to changes in the value of convertible notes and other instruments used to raise funding, rather than operating costs.

The scale of Anthropic’s infrastructure commitments is the filing’s most striking feature. According to the Journal, the company owes around $450 billion under cloud agreements over the next seven to 10 years, most of which cannot be cancelled. That includes about $111 billion with Google, $110 billion with Amazon Web Services and $31 billion with Microsoft, plus up to $86 billion for Nvidia chip capacity from Nscale and Lambda. A separate obligation of more than $160 billion to lease Google chips through Broadcom lifts the total above $600 billion, and deals still under negotiation could add up to $150 billion more.

Even so, the company said its major cloud partners had not provided as much capacity as it sought, and that those partners increasingly view it as a competitor. Anthropic is supplementing that capacity with leased data centres and third-party operators, some of which it said have short track records.

Revenue is also concentrated. Two customers accounted for about a fifth of first-half sales, and the company expects a large share of revenue to keep coming from a small group of clients.

Risk factors make up roughly a third of the document, the Journal reported. They include the possibility of misaligned AI models causing harm, liability for damages such as data theft, and incidents severe enough that insurance may not cover them. Anthropic also cited increasingly coordinated political opposition to data centre construction, noting that its public profile could draw attention to projects linked to it.

The filing comes as Anthropic prepares for a listing that could value it at up to $2 trillion, putting its growth rate, cost base and customer mix under far closer public scrutiny than before.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Boeing wins FAA approval for 737 MAX 10, unlocking nearly 1,500 orders after 7-year wait
item.description:
Certification removes one of the largest overhangs on Boeing’s stock, given how sharply shares reacted to the last delay, falling nearly 7% in late September when a software glitch put approval on hold. The bigger financial prize is cash flow: Boeing has been carrying dozens of completed but undelivered MAX 7 and MAX 10 jets, and converting that inventory into deliveries should support cash generation over the next year or more. Attention now shifts to Boeing’s third-quarter results on 27 October, where investors will look for a delivery timeline and any update to cash flow guidance. For Airbus, the approval ends a long period in which the A321neo faced no direct rival at the top of the single-aisle market.

---

Seven years late and one software scare later, Boeing finally has its answer to the A321neo cleared to fly, and with it a large backlog it can at last start turning into cash.

Summary:

  • The FAA granted final certification to the 737 MAX 10 on Tuesday, the largest variant of Boeing’s best-selling jet family
  • The approval clears the way for deliveries against nearly 1,500 orders, about 30% of the 737 backlog
  • United Airlines is the largest customer with 167 firm orders; Alaska Airlines holds 105, with Ryanair, Delta and American also major buyers
  • The first MAX 10 rolled out in November 2019 and was originally due to enter service in 2020
  • Delays stemmed from the 2019 to 2020 MAX grounding, tighter FAA oversight, an engine anti-ice flaw and, most recently, a software issue disclosed in September
  • The aircraft seats 185 to 230 passengers with a range of about 3,100 nautical miles

The US Federal Aviation Administration has certified Boeing’s 737 MAX 10, clearing the largest model in the planemaker’s best-selling jet family for customer deliveries after a delay of almost seven years. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was scheduled to mark the approval at Boeing’s factory in Everett, Washington, on Tuesday.

The decision unlocks close to 1,500 orders, roughly 30% of Boeing’s total 737 backlog. United Airlines is the largest customer, with 167 firm orders, followed by Alaska Airlines with 105. Ryanair, Delta Air Lines and American Airlines are also significant buyers. The MAX 10 seats between 185 and 230 passengers and flies about 3,100 nautical miles, positioning it against the Airbus A321neo at the top end of the single-aisle market.

The first MAX 10 rolled off the line in November 2019, with service entry originally planned for 2020. The programme was then caught up in the worldwide MAX grounding that followed two fatal crashes, tighter certification standards and closer FAA scrutiny after a door panel blew out of a 737 MAX 9 in flight in January 2024. A flaw in the engine anti-ice system, identified in 2023, added further delay because running the system continuously could overheat the engine inlet.

The final stretch was not smooth either. In late September, Boeing disclosed a software issue that could prevent pilots from using automated flight guidance in a specific landing scenario, and the FAA said it would hold off on approval until the problem was resolved, according to Reuters. Boeing shares fell close to 7% that day. The regulator later allowed certification to proceed while Boeing works on a permanent software update. Flight testing had already been completed in July, after nearly 1,000 flights and more than 2,060 hours in the air.

The approval follows certification of the smaller MAX 7 in August. Boeing said in its most recent quarterly filing that it held about 40 completed MAX 7 and MAX 10 aircraft in inventory at the end of June, and chief executive Kelly Ortberg has said the company expects to work through stored jets of both models over roughly 18 months.

Production capacity is also building. Boeing opened a new 737 line in Everett in July to supplement output in Renton, and is moving its 737 production rate from 42 to 47 aircraft a month, with further increases planned. The new Everett line must be production-certified by the FAA before it can deliver aircraft.

Analysts have long seen MAX 10 deliveries as critical to restoring Boeing’s revenue and cash flow. The company reports third-quarter results on 27 October, when investors will be watching for a firm delivery schedule and any change to its cash flow outlook. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
